Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette: These potent reminders often led her to immediately pull over and call her sister, or to simply turn around and avoid the route altogether, reinforcing her belief that driving was too dangerous. The persistent, vivid nature of these memories made her acutely sensitive to any remotely similar sensory input, turning previously innocuous sounds like distant sirens into potent triggers for panic. By consistently sidestepping these potential reminders, she inadvertently prevented herself from habituating to them, thus maintaining their power as potent triggers. Such sounds would instantly flood her mind with fragmented, terrifying images of the impact and the shattered windshield, as if reliving the event in real-time. Each encounter with a trigger solidified her conviction that the world was an inherently unsafe place and that she was constantly vulnerable to harm. This deep-seated conviction that she was flawed and the world was dangerous kept her in a perpetual state of hypervigilance, constantly scanning for any sign of impending threat. These vivid re-experiences made her feel as though the danger was still present, immediately intensifying her physical sensations of threat and making her heart race. This perpetual state of alert made it incredibly difficult for her to process the traumatic event in a coherent way, leaving the memory fragmented and prone to intrusive re-experiencing. These efforts to suppress and avoid processing the event meant the traumatic memory remained fragmented and poorly integrated, making it more likely to intrude spontaneously. Her persistent feeling of being unsafe, even in her own apartment, only served to reinforce her deepest negative appraisal: that she was indeed permanently damaged and unable to protect herself. However, each time she chose avoidance, it subtly reinforced her negative appraisal that she was incapable of coping with the outside world, further cementing her belief in her own fragility. This reliance on avoidance prevented her from learning that many situations were actually safe, thereby perpetuating her heightened sense of threat and keeping her on edge.
